```
[princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp)
# Today ## Goals

- Familiarity with the core of the tidyverse for data manipulation - Ability to use `tibble`, `dplyr`, and `purrr` over base R equivalents - Practice with actual datasets in R - Tomorrow: `ggplot2` ## Sources

- Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund, *R for Data Science*, 2e - [Ch. 3: Data transformation](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html) (especially §§3.1-3.5) - [Ch. 19: Joins](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html) (especially §§19.2-19.3) - [Ch. 26: Iteration](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration.html) (especially §§26.2-26.3) - Harvard IQSS, *Math Prefresher for Political Scientists* - [Ch. 9: Objects, Functions, Loops](https://iqss.github.io/prefresher/13_functions_obj_loops.html) - [Ch. 11: Joins and Merges](https://iqss.github.io/prefresher/15_project-dempeace.html) # The tidyverse ## The tidyverse

- A collection of R packages for data science - Packages designed around tidy data - each observation is a row and each column is a variable - Core packages today: `tibble`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `purrr`
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: ::: fragment ```r ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ✔ dplyr 1.2.1 ✔ readr 2.2.0 ✔ forcats 1.0.1 ✔ stringr 1.6.0 ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3 ✔ tibble 3.3.1 ✔ lubridate 1.9.5 ✔ tidyr 1.3.2 ✔ purrr 1.2.2 ── Conflicts ──────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ℹ Use the conflicted package to force all conflicts to become errors ``` ::: ## Tibble

- A tibble is a data frame with more predictable behavior - Printing shows the first rows and the columns that fit - Column types appear below the column names ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 7 GEOID state county income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 01001 Alabama Autauga County 69841 5512 1200 75 2 01003 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 2751 1211 42 3 01005 Alabama Barbour County 44290 2762 644 41 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Tibble

![](figs/tibble.jpg){fig-align="center" height="560"} ## Printing a tibble

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 7 GEOID state county income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 01001 Alabama Autauga County 69841 5512 1200 75 2 01003 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 2751 1211 42 3 01005 Alabama Barbour County 44290 2762 644 41 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Tibble printing

![](figs/tibble_printing.jpeg){fig-align="center" height="560"} ## Creating a tibble

- `tibble()` builds a data frame from named columns - Columns have equal length or length one ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_respondents <- tibble( id = c(101L, 102L, 103L), party = c("Democrat", "Independent", "Republican"), trust_government = c(3L, 5L, 2L) ) ``` :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(id = seq_len(3L), enrolled = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 id enrolled 1 1 TRUE 2 2 TRUE 3 3 TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Inspecting a tibble

Inspect before transforming data - `glimpse()` displays each column and its type - `names()` returns column names - `dim()` returns rows and columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(state, county, income, rent) |> glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 3,144 Columns: 4 $ state "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alaba… $ county "Autauga County", "Baldwin County", "Barbour County", "Bibb C… $ income 69841, 75019, 44290, 51215, 61096, 36723, 44881, 55826, 49295… $ rent 1200, 1211, 644, 802, 743, 635, 722, 804, 850, 750, 855, 653,… ``` ::: ::: ## Extracting a column

`$` and `[[` return a column as a vector ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(counties$income) class(counties[["income"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Both approaches return a vector ::: ::: fragment `[` instead returns a one-column tibble ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(counties["income"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ``` ::: ::: # Data transformation ## `dplyr` verbs

::: incremental - Rows - `filter()` / `slice()`: subset to specific rows - `arrange()`: reorder by a variable - Columns - `select()`: subset to specific columns - `mutate()`: create or update columns - `rename()`: rename specific columns - Groups - `group_by()`: identify groupings in data - `summarize()`: reduce groups to summaries ::: ## `filter()`

`filter()` keeps rows that satisfy a logical condition ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(income >= 75000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 716 × 7 GEOID state county income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 01003 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 2751 1211 42 2 01051 Alabama Elmore County 75553 3115 1014 48 3 01083 Alabama Limestone County 83534 2861 908 49 # ℹ 713 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Multiple conditions: equivalent to AND

Commas require every condition to be `TRUE` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(state == "New York", income >= 75000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 19 × 7 GEOID state county income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 36001 New York Albany County 83149 1788 1252 22 2 36021 New York Columbia County 83619 3965 1199 45 3 36027 New York Dutchess County 97273 2529 1522 45 # ℹ 16 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment which is the same as: ```r counties |> filter(state == "New York") |> filter(income >= 75000) ``` ::: ::: fragment which is the same as ```r counties |> filter(state == "New York" & income >= 75000) ``` ::: ## Missing values

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- tibble(id = 1:4, score = c(88L, NA, 91L, 76L)) ``` ::: ::: fragment What happens with NAs? ```r scores |> filter(score > 90) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 id score 1 3 91 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `arrange()`

- `arrange()` orders rows by one or more columns - Use `desc()` for descending order ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> arrange(desc(income)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 7 GEOID state county income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 51107 Virginia Loudoun County 178707 3411 2317 39 2 06085 California Santa Clara County 159674 1962 2814 16 3 06081 California San Mateo County 156000 3019 2893 36 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## `slice_*()`: rows by position or rank

- `slice_head()` / `slice_tail()`: the first or last rows - `slice_min()` / `slice_max()`: the smallest or largest by a column - `slice_sample()`: a random draw of rows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> slice_max(income, n = 3) |> select(state, county, income) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 state county income 1 Virginia Loudoun County 178707 2 California Santa Clara County 159674 3 California San Mateo County 156000 ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Each takes `n =` for a count of rows or `prop =` for a share of them ::: ## `slice_*()` respects groups

`by =` groups for this one call -- here, the richest county in each state: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> slice_max(income, n = 1, by = state) |> select(state, county, income) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 51 × 3 state county income 1 Alabama Shelby County 93543 2 Alaska Aleutians West Census Area 107344 3 Arizona Maricopa County 85518 # ℹ 48 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment The same as `group_by(state) |> slice_max(income, n = 1) |> ungroup()` ::: ## `distinct()`

`distinct()` keeps unique values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> distinct(state) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 51 × 1 state 1 Alabama 2 Alaska 3 Arizona # ℹ 48 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Use multiple columns for unique combinations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> distinct(state, county) |> nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3144 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `select()`

`select()` keeps, drops, or reorders columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(state, county, income, rent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 4 state county income rent 1 Alabama Autauga County 69841 1200 2 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 1211 3 Alabama Barbour County 44290 644 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## `select()`: ranges and exclusions

We can also select with ranges ... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(state:income) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "state" "county" "income" ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment ... and with exclusions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(-c(income_moe, rent_moe)) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "GEOID" "state" "county" "income" "rent" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Selection helpers

We can select based on names using `starts_with()`, `ends_with()`, and `contains()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(starts_with("rent")) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "rent" "rent_moe" ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Or with a helper function inside `where()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "income" "income_moe" "rent" "rent_moe" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `rename()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> rename( median_renter_income = income, median_gross_rent = rent ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 7 GEOID state county median_renter_income income_moe median_gross_rent 1 01001 Alabama Autauga Cou… 69841 5512 1200 2 01003 Alabama Baldwin Cou… 75019 2751 1211 3 01005 Alabama Barbour Cou… 44290 2762 644 # ℹ 3,141 more rows # ℹ 1 more variable: rent_moe ``` ::: ::: ## `relocate()`

Move columns to the front: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> relocate(income, rent) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "income" "rent" "GEOID" "state" "county" [6] "income_moe" "rent_moe" ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Or to a specific location: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> relocate(county, .after = state) |> names() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "GEOID" "state" "county" "income" "income_moe" [6] "rent" "rent_moe" ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `mutate()`

`mutate()` creates new columns or replaces old ones ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> mutate( income_thousands = income / 1000, rent_hundreds = rent / 100 ) |> select(state, county, income_thousands, rent_hundreds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 4 state county income_thousands rent_hundreds 1 Alabama Autauga County 69.8 12 2 Alabama Baldwin County 75.0 12.1 3 Alabama Barbour County 44.3 6.44 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Keeping only specific columns

`.keep = "none"` keeps only the updated columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> mutate( income_thousands = income / 1000, rent_hundreds = rent / 100, .keep = "none" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 2 income_thousands rent_hundreds 1 69.8 12 2 75.0 12.1 3 44.3 6.44 # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Before 2025, this was `transmute()` ::: ## Conditional variables: `if_else()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> mutate( rent_level = if_else( rent >= median(rent, na.rm = TRUE), "at or above median", "below median" ) ) |> select(state, county, rent, rent_level) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 4 state county rent rent_level 1 Alabama Autauga County 1200 at or above median 2 Alabama Baldwin County 1211 at or above median 3 Alabama Barbour County 644 below median # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Complex conditional variables: `case_when()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> mutate( income_group = case_when( is.na(income) ~ "missing", income >= 100000 ~ "high", income >= 75000 ~ "middle", .default = "low" ) ) |> select(state, county, income, income_group) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 4 state county income income_group 1 Alabama Autauga County 69841 low 2 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 middle 3 Alabama Barbour County 44290 low # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Exercise

- Keep counties in New York or Texas - Create `income_thousands` from `income` - Keep `state`, `county`, `income`, and `income_thousands` - Order from highest to lowest income
Write this as one pipeline ## A solution

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(state %in% c("New York", "Texas")) |> mutate(income_thousands = income / 1000) |> select(state, county, income, income_thousands) |> arrange(desc(income)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 316 × 4 state county income income_thousands 1 New York Nassau County 143408 143. 2 New York Suffolk County 128329 128. 3 New York Putnam County 127405 127. # ℹ 313 more rows ``` ::: ::: # Strings with `stringr` ## Common `stringr` functions

Every function starts with `str_` and takes the string as its first argument - `str_length()`: how many characters - `str_to_lower()`, `str_to_upper()`, `str_to_title()`: change case - `str_c()`: glue strings together - `str_sub()`: pull out characters by position - `str_trim()`, `str_squish()`: drop stray whitespace ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> mutate(label = str_to_lower(str_c(county, ", ", state))) |> select(label) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 1 label 1 autauga county, alabama 2 baldwin county, alabama 3 barbour county, alabama # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Detecting and replacing patterns

- `str_detect()`: does the string contain the pattern? Returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` - `str_starts()`, `str_ends()`: match at one end only - `str_remove()`, `str_replace()`: change the first match - `str_remove_all()`, `str_replace_all()`: change every match ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(str_detect(county, "Parish")) |> mutate(parish = str_remove(county, " Parish$")) |> select(state, parish) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 64 × 2 state parish 1 Louisiana Acadia 2 Louisiana Allen 3 Louisiana Ascension # ℹ 61 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Patterns are *regular expressions*: `^` anchors to the start and `$` to the end. Wrap a pattern in `fixed()` to match it literally. ::: # Pivots in tidyr ## Long and wide data

:::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Wide data** Each observation is a row ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wide <- tribble( ~id, ~v1, ~v2, ~v3, "A", 100L, 120L, 105L, "B", 80L, 90L, 90L ) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Long data** Observations are split across rows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} long <- tribble( ~id, ~statistic, ~value, "A", "v1", 100L, "A", "v2", 120L, "A", "v3", 105L, "B", "v1", 80L, "B", "v2", 90L, "B", "v3", 90L, ) ``` ::: ::: :::: ## `pivot_wider()`

`pivot_wider()` shortens the data by adding columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} long |> pivot_wider( names_from = statistic, values_from = value ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 id v1 v2 v3 1 A 100 120 105 2 B 80 90 90 ``` ::: ::: ## `pivot_longer()`

`pivot_longer()` lengthens the data by turning columns into rows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wide |> pivot_longer( cols = v1:v3, names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 3 id statistic value 1 A v1 100 2 A v2 120 3 A v3 105 # ℹ 3 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Other weird data shapes

- Most can be *tidied* with `tidyr` - Nested data? Some variables are lists - `unnest()`, `unnest_wider()`, `unnest_longer()` - Data should be nested? - Are you sure? - `nest()` - Handle `NA` values - `drop_na()` or `replace_na()` - Missing within groups: `fill()` - Missing combinations (e.g., all weeks should have 7 days) - `expand()` for new data or `complete()` to supplement # Groups and summaries ## `summarize()`

`summarize()` reduces rows to summary values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> summarize( n = n(), mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), median_rent = median(rent, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 n mean_income median_rent 1 3144 66073. 854 ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment `n()` counts the rows in the current group. It takes no arguments, and only works inside `dplyr` verbs, where "the current group" has a meaning. ::: ::: fragment If there are no groups, `summarize()` treats all rows as one group ::: ## `group_by()`

`group_by()` marks a `tibble` as having groups ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> group_by(state) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), median_rent = median(rent, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 51 × 4 state n mean_income median_rent 1 Alabama 67 54196. 762 2 Alaska 30 79407. 1243 3 Arizona 15 62663. 983 # ℹ 48 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Grouped mutation

`mutate()` will respect groups for vectorized operations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> group_by(state) |> mutate( income_difference = income - mean(income, na.rm = TRUE) ) |> select(state, county, income, income_difference) |> ungroup() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 4 state county income income_difference 1 Alabama Autauga County 69841 15645. 2 Alabama Baldwin County 75019 20823. 3 Alabama Barbour County 44290 -9906. # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## `count()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> count(state) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 51 × 2 state n 1 Alabama 67 2 Alaska 30 3 Arizona 15 # ℹ 48 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment `count(state)` groups by `state` and counts rows Equivalent to: ```r counties |> group_by(state) |> summarize(n = n()) ``` ::: ## Multiple summaries: `across()`

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> summarize( across( c(income, rent), list( mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) ) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 income_mean income_sd rent_mean rent_sd 1 66073. 17387. 938. 302. ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment `across()` applies the same functions to several columns ::: ## Multiple summaries: `across()`

`across()` simplifies making summaries: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> summarize(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 income income_moe rent rent_moe 1 66073. 5068. 938. 73.6 ``` ::: ::: ## Exercise

Compare counties above and below the median income. - Exclude counties with missing `income` - Label counties as `at or above median` or `below median` - For each group, report `n` and the mean `income` and `rent` using `across()`
Write this as one pipeline ## A solution

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sol <- counties |> filter(!is.na(income)) |> mutate( income_level = if_else( income >= median(income), "at or above median", "below median" ) ) |> group_by(income_level) |> summarize( n = n(), across(c(income, rent), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop" ) |> arrange(desc(income)) ``` ::: ## A solution

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sol ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 income_level n income rent 1 at or above median 1571 78668. 1090. 2 below median 1571 53479. 787. ``` ::: ::: # Joins ## Join tables by a fixed key

- A join combines columns from related tables - A key identifies which rows should match ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} party <- tibble( id = c(101L, 102L, 103L), party = c("Democrat", "Independent", "Republican") ) attitudes <- tibble( id = c(101L, 102L, 104L), trust_government = c(3L, 5L, 2L) ) ``` ::: ::: fragment A key is (often) just a numeric ID ::: ## Check the key

A key should identify the intended unit of observation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} attitudes |> count(id) |> filter(n > 1L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 0 × 2 # ℹ 2 variables: id , n ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment An empty result means no duplicate keys were found ::: ## Left and right tables

```{=html}

left

idparty
101Democrat
102Independent
103Republican
104Democrat
106Republican

right

idtrust
1025
1033
1042
1054
1067
``` ## Types of joins

::: incremental - `left_join()`: keep all rows in left and add columns from right - `right_join()`: keep all rows in right and add columns from left - `inner_join()` keeps rows matched in both tables - `full_join()` keeps rows from either table - `semi_join()` keeps left rows with a match - `anti_join()` keeps left rows without a match ::: ::: fragment Which rows are saved for each join? ```r left |> *_join(by = "id") ``` ::: ## Joining real data

`counties` and `county_pop` use different names for the same key ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties_joined <- counties |> left_join(county_pop, join_by(GEOID == fips)) counties_joined |> select(GEOID, state, county, pop, region, division) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,144 × 6 GEOID state county pop region division 1 01001 Alabama Autauga County 58805 South East South Central 2 01003 Alabama Baldwin County 231767 South East South Central 3 01005 Alabama Barbour County 25223 South East South Central # ℹ 3,141 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Joining real data: multiple syntaxes

Current, recommended syntax: ```r counties_joined <- counties |> left_join(county_pop, join_by(GEOID == fips)) ``` ::: fragment Older, but also valid syntax: ```r counties_joined <- counties |> left_join(county_pop, by = c("GEOID" = "fips")) ``` ::: ::: fragment Most replication data (and many of your colleagues) will use the older syntax! ::: ::: fragment New syntax allows for *fancier* joins, like `join_by(x > x)`... ::: ## Find unmatched keys

Check the rows that do not match: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(GEOID, state, county) |> anti_join(county_pop, join_by(GEOID == fips)) |> select(GEOID, state, county) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 9 × 3 GEOID state county 1 09110 Connecticut Capitol Planning Region 2 09120 Connecticut Greater Bridgeport Planning Region 3 09130 Connecticut Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Region # ℹ 6 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment What's wrong with Connecticut? ::: ## Duplicate keys change row counts

A join can duplicate left rows when the right key is not unique ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} attitudes_duplicate <- tibble( id = c(101L, 101L, 102L), trust_government = c(3L, 4L, 5L) ) party |> left_join(attitudes_duplicate, join_by(id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 id party trust_government 1 101 Democrat 3 2 101 Democrat 4 3 102 Independent 5 # ℹ 1 more row ``` ::: ::: # `purrr` ## `map()`

`map(x, f)` is a new way to do yesterday's `lapply(x, f)` ::: fragment Why `map()` then? Large family of *type-stable* `map_*()` functions! ::: ::: fragment And bits of friendlier syntax: ```r lapply(x, `[[`, "a") map(x, "a") ``` ::: ## Typed maps

Typed maps return a vector of a *known* type: - `map_dbl()`: double vector - `map_int()`: integer vector - `map_chr()`: character vector - `map_lgl()`: logical vector ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> select(income, rent) |> map_dbl( \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` income rent 66073.0945 938.1388 ``` ::: ::: ## Mapping over data frames

Create a list of `tibble`s with `group_split()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counties_by_region <- counties_joined |> filter(!is.na(region)) |> group_by(region) |> group_split() ``` ::: ::: fragment `map_dbl()` then returns one value per `tibble`: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} map_dbl( counties_by_region, \(x) mean(x$income, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 67678.39 78195.17 60859.68 72626.80 ``` ::: ::: ## Combining results

First return one tibble for each region ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summaries <- map( counties_by_region, function(data) { summarize( data, n = n(), mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE) ) } ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all(map_lgl(summaries, is_tibble)) length(summaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: ## Stack compatible results

`list_rbind()` combines the tibbles by row ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} list_rbind(summaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 n mean_income 1 1055 67678. 2 209 78195. 3 1422 60860. # ℹ 1 more row ``` ::: ::: ## Stacking with `bind_rows()`

`bind_rows()` stacks data frames too, and `.id =` records where each row came from ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(summaries) <- map_chr(counties_by_region, \(x) x$region[[1]]) bind_rows(summaries, .id = "region") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 region n mean_income 1 Midwest 1055 67678. 2 Northeast 209 78195. 3 South 1422 60860. # ℹ 1 more row ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment `.id` takes its values from the *names* of the list. An unnamed list gets `"1"`, `"2"`, ... instead -- so name the list first if you want the column to mean anything. ::: ## Several inputs

`map2()` iterates over two (equal length) inputs in parallel ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} district_turnout <- list(c(0.62, 0.58, 0.64), c(0.71, 0.69, 0.74)) benchmarks <- c(0.60, 0.70) map2_lgl( district_turnout, benchmarks, \(turnout, benchmark) mean(turnout) > benchmark ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: ## `walk()`: mapping for the side effect

`walk()` calls a function for what it *does* -- write a file, print, save a plot -- and hands back its input invisibly ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} walk(c("Northeast", "South"), \(region) cat("Region:", region, "\n")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Region: Northeast Region: South ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment Reach for it when the return value is not the point: ```r iwalk(summaries, \(data, name) write_csv(data, str_c(name, ".csv"))) ``` `walk2()` pairs two lists, and `iwalk()` pairs a list with its names ::: ## Progress bars

Every `map()` and `walk()` takes a `.progress` argument ```r counties_by_region |> map(slow_summary, .progress = TRUE) ``` ::: fragment Pass a string instead of `TRUE` to label the bar: ```r counties_by_region |> map(slow_summary, .progress = "summarizing regions") ``` ::: ::: fragment Worth it when a map runs long enough that you want to know it is still going ::: ## Running in parallel

Wrap the function in `in_parallel()` to spread a map across worker processes: ```r library(mirai) daemons(4) # start four workers counties_by_region |> map(in_parallel(\(data) mean(data$income, na.rm = TRUE))) daemons(0) # shut them down ``` ::: fragment Without `daemons()`, it quietly falls back to running sequentially ::: ## Parallel functions must be self-contained

The function gets shipped to another process, so it cannot see your workspace - Call package functions with `::`, as in `dplyr::summarize()` - Pass any data it needs as named arguments to `in_parallel()` ```r counties_by_region |> map(in_parallel( \(data) dplyr::filter(data, income > cutoff), cutoff = 75000 )) ``` ::: fragment Still experimental, and only pays off when each call is genuinely slow -- shipping data between processes is not free ::: # Applied exercise ## Exercise

Using `counties_joined`, compare income by region and population level - Label counties as above or below the median population - Compute the number of counties and mean income by `region` and population level - Order the summary from highest to lowest mean income ::: fragment
Write one pipeline ::: ## Step 1: label population

```r counties_labeled <- counties_joined |> mutate( pop_level = # ... ) ``` ::: fragment Use `if_else()` or `case_when()` ::: ## Step 2: summarize groups

```r result <- counties_labeled |> # group by region and population level # summarize n and mean_income # arrange by descending mean_income ``` ::: fragment How many rows should the result contain? ::: ## One possible solution

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- counties_joined |> filter(!is.na(pop), !is.na(region)) |> mutate( pop_level = if_else( pop >= median(pop), "at or above median", "below median" ) ) |> group_by(region, pop_level) |> summarize( n = n(), mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) |> arrange(desc(mean_income)) ``` ::: ## Apply a function to each group

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} region_summary <- function(data) { data |> summarize( n = n(), mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), median_rent = median(rent, na.rm = TRUE) ) } ``` ::: ::: fragment Apply `region_summary()` to each region with `map()` ::: ## One possible solution

::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_region <- counties_joined |> filter(!is.na(region)) |> group_by(region) |> group_split() by_region |> map(region_summary) |> list_rbind() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 n mean_income median_rent 1 1055 67678. 804 2 209 78195. 1056 3 1422 60860. 845 # ℹ 1 more row ``` ::: ::: ## Other tidyverse packages

- `stringr` works with character strings - `lubridate` parses and transforms dates and times - `forcats` works with categorical variables ("factors") - `readr` imports rectangular data files ## Summary

- Start with a tibble and inspect its rows, columns, and types - Use one `dplyr` verb for each transformation - Use pipes to connect transformations - Group before computing group-level summaries - Check keys before and after joins - Use `map()` to apply a function to every list element

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
